title: Rubric for reviewing a third-party AI test report (LLM applications)

scale.1: Mentioned or partly done, but not specific enough for a reviewer to check it.
scale.2: Done and stated specifically enough that a reviewer could check or repeat it.

rules: Score only what the document under review states. An indicator the report does not address scores 0 and becomes an evidence request, not a finding that the work was not done.
Every score above 0 cites the page and a short quotation (at most 25 words). Every score of 0 says what was looked for.
Indicators marked critical are the ones without which a reported result cannot be relied on. A report with a critical indicator at 0 is referred back for evidence, whatever its total.
Criterion totals are reported separately. The overall total is a summary only, because a high score in one criterion does not offset a missing critical indicator in another.

indicators.text: Risks are selected for the use case and the selection is justified (deployment context, users, severity).
Each material risk has output tests, and component tests (retrieval, filters, system prompt) where they are needed to explain or confirm results.
Test data represent the application: realistic inputs, breadth and depth, edge cases, the languages and user types the application serves.
What was not tested, and why, is stated.
Metrics measure the stated objective and fit the data format (e.g. precision and recall of facts, attack success rate).
Automated evaluators (rules, classifiers, LLM judges) are checked against human or gold labels on a sample, and the agreement is reported.
Pass thresholds are set before testing, with a stated basis.
Helpfulness or over-refusal on legitimate requests is measured alongside safety.
The system under test is identified: version or build, underlying model, configuration, test dates and environment.
The test set is released, or its construction is described well enough to rebuild an equivalent one.
Evaluator configuration is stated: judge model, rubric or prompt, decision rule.
Tests are repeated, at least on a subset, and run-to-run variation is reported.
The number of test cases behind each reported result is given.
Uncertainty is reported: confidence intervals, variance across runs, or an equivalent.
Comparisons (between languages, versions, techniques) give both rates and their sample sizes, or a test, and claims stay within what the sample supports.
Results are broken down by sub-category (topic, harm type, data type, attack technique).
Quantitative results are reported for each tested risk, against the thresholds where there are thresholds.
Failure cases are analysed qualitatively, with examples.
Limitations of the test and the residual risk to the application are stated.
Recommendations are specific and say what should be re-tested.
